title: The softest thing
hookLine: the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest (Tao Te Ching 43)

cards: Under an old gutter spout, the concrete has a shallow bowl worn into it. Nobody chiseled it. Nobody planned it.
Rain did it, one drop after another, season after season, on the same patch of ground. The concrete is harder than any raindrop. The concrete still lost.
Chapter forty-three of the Tao Te Ching opens on that kind of quiet victory, and then it adds something new.

teach.b: First, the line. In James Legge's translation, chapter forty-three begins: "The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest."
Last week, chapter thirty-six said the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. This chapter says it again, then goes somewhere new. Second, the new thing.

teach.h: IT ENTERS WHERE THERE'S NO CRACK.
teach.b: What has no substance, it says, can enter where there is no crack at all. Water doesn't need a door. It finds its way into the stone, the soil, the root.
The softest thing doesn't win by smashing through. It gets in where nothing hard could. Third, a way of teaching.
The chapter says this shows the benefit of not forcing, and it speaks of a teaching without words. Then it adds, plainly, that few in the world reach it.
That's an honest admission inside the book itself: this is hard to live. Fourth, the hard places in a life. A teenager who won't talk.
A coworker braced for an argument. An old family wound. Pushing harder doesn't always open them.
The chapter's picture is different: steady, gentle, repeated presence, the way rain keeps falling on the same spot.
A kind word every day. A meal left without comment. In this reading, the soft way doesn't break the stone.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often turn to chapter forty-three's image of water on stone when a situation won't yield to force, choosing steady, gentle persistence instead.

o: the weakest person, who always loses in the end
a gentle word that hides a sharp threat inside
the yielding that wears down the hard and gets inside it

p: worn into a bowl by rain

s: chapter forty-three says the soft wins by smashing through
it wins by entering where there's no crack at all.
the chapter admits that few in the world reach this
an honest note inside the book: it's hard to live.
chapter forty-three is the only place the book says soft overcomes hard

games.q: a coworker is braced for an argument every time you speak. what does chapter forty-three's picture suggest?
o: argue harder until they give in.
steady, gentle presence, again and again.
stop speaking to them at all.
games.why: the chapter's softest thing doesn't break the stone. like rain on the same spot, it gets in where force can't.

practice: If you can, let a thin stream of water run over a pebble, a spoon or the back of your hand; if not, close your eyes and picture a river over rocks, or rain on a step.
Watch how the water doesn't argue with what's in its way: it goes around, over, into. Let your breath move like that, soft and steady, without pushing.

wordCard.voice: The softest thing. Chapter forty-three: the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest, and enters where there is no crack. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: no gap, no crevice; in chapter forty-three, what has no substance enters where there is 無間.

carryVoice: Your line: the softest. Rain never hurries, and still the stone gives way to it. Until tomorrow.
